e79c330ad8: Extended notes: where the guitar came from
76d7f5c9dd: The guitar is a plucked string instrument whose ancestry goes back to the oud of the Middle East. In Europe the oud became the lute, and in Spain the vihuela developed. Early guitars had strings in pairs called "courses"; Renaissance guitars had four courses, the five-course guitar appeared in the 16th century and gradually replaced it, and in the late 18th century the paired strings became six single strings, forming today's six-string guitar.
65ac3e2511: Extended notes: how the guitar changed
f61b384bef: The four-course guitar used gut strings; the five-course guitar appeared
1c0ae84437: The five-course guitar was popular at court and among ordinary people; the lute slowly left the stage
cbdc709a64: The six-string guitar takes shape; F. Sor, D. Aguado, M. Carcassi and others left a large body of pieces and method books
8c2abcd95e: The piano took centre stage and fewer composers wrote for guitar; F. Tárrega brought the guitar back into favour through his playing and arrangements
6cffea5db0: Spanish luthier A. de Torres enlarged the body, set the string length at about 65 cm and used fan bracing, creating the model for the modern classical guitar
a7f58e4eba: A. Segovia championed it all his life; J. Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez put the guitar on the concerto stage
8134d749b9: Blues, country and folk rose in America; Martin and other makers switched to steel strings and strengthened the body for a brighter, louder sound
3fe842978a: Pickups turn string vibration into an electrical signal; in 1950 Leo Fender released a mass-produced solid-body electric guitar
d056585a5e: For three hundred years, nearly every change to the guitar has been about volume, so it can be heard clearly in a band.
60a728c639: A wide neck, played solo with the fingers, with a focus on technique and staff notation; usually played seated with the guitar on the left leg
920dd7f2e7: From Andalusia in Spain, with a lighter body and bright tone; often played with dance, castanets and singing
2eed23c13b: All steel; strings 1–2 plain, strings 3–6 wound
6e9916a62e: A bright tone and plenty of volume; accompanies pop songs with chords and a capo, and can be played fingerstyle too
6e4b8bb06e: Makes its sound through pickups and an amplifier; split into lead and rhythm, with the electric bass handling the low end
e961e88bab: Laid flat on the lap, the left hand slides a steel bar and the right hand wears finger picks, for a long, singing sound
73beceb0cb: The four-string ukulele, the round-headed banjo, and the mandolin, whose back looks like half a pear
af5c89a7a6: Extended notes: parts of the guitar

250cfb4b2d: Hold the strings and tune them; sealed (oil-filled) and open types are common
85b4bff2c5: Sets the string spacing; the harder the material, the less vibration is lost; bone, plastic and Tusq are common
bc614cc0cf: Where the left hand presses the strings, usually rosewood, ebony or maple
39d764bfa0: Keep the pitch steady once a string is pressed; usually brass or stainless steel
cd690b9699: Markers at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12; fret 12 is an octave above the open string
1af54ae287: Joins the headstock to the body, with a truss rod inside
4bd88c5cb8: The main source of the tone
ce02165a89: Once the air inside the body resonates, the sound comes out here
e1f505e3ce: Decorates and reinforces the edge of the sound hole
c9031247dc: Stops the top getting scratched when you strum
2c02fb1c1a: Takes the strings' pull and passes their vibration to the top

c4180cac9f: Hold the string ends in the bridge

dd72df398d: The sound's path: the right hand plucks → the string vibrates → saddle and bridge → the top vibrates → the air inside the body resonates → out through the sound hole.
3a6755b28c: Extended notes: what the body is made of
366be21aa5: **Laminated**: pressed from thin wood sheets with glue layers. Affordable and not easily affected by temperature and humidity; the glue absorbs vibration, so resonance is weaker.
d549390ba1: **Solid**: made from a single piece of wood. A more open sound that "opens up" further after years of playing; more expensive, and you need to watch the humidity. Only a solid top is called a "solid top"; a solid top, sides and back is called "all solid".
a3f16099be: How to tell: look at the edge of the top through the sound hole. If the top and bottom layers are different colours with a layer in between, it's most likely laminated; if the grain runs through in one piece, it's solid.
fa7183a077: Pale yellow and hard; bright and clear, the most common on folk guitars
1b15403294: Dark orange-brown and soft; warm, round and quick to vibrate, common on classical guitars
193e5bc051: Deep lows, bright highs, rich overtones
c12bf9ca51: Clean and direct; doesn't get buried by other instruments in a band
5daf39ee60: Sweet upper mids that sound better the more it's played
1cb8b1f8d1: Light, soft and affordable, with gentle mids
6082225bd1: The same wood also varies with origin, thickness and workmanship; the table is only for comparison.
f69428abd6: Extended notes: size and body shape
7b4ddbb419: Choose a size to fit your body: about 1/4 for ages 2–5, 1/2 for 5–8, 3/4 for 8–12, and full size from 12 up to adults. If your right arm rests naturally on the top edge of the body and your straight left arm reaches fret 1, the size is right.
3fba179f12: Widest at the bottom and narrowest at the waist; full bass and the most volume
1d5e44f652: The most common; square shoulders, loud, with an even frequency balance
bfa113e05f: Clear mids, good for both strumming and fingerstyle
0d42dbad3e: A slim waist with distinct highs and lows; good for fingerstyle and recording
8418260593: A compact body with responsive highs; good for fingerstyle and lead
8b1f9530df: The smallest and lightest, easy to carry
fa6b24038a: Each brand has its own body specs; holding and playing one yourself is the real test.
594c4d2b25: **Bracing**: wooden strips glued under the top that support the strings' pull and shape how the top vibrates. Folk guitars use X bracing to handle steel-string tension; classical guitars use the fan bracing Torres established.
01bb93ce7d: **Truss rod**: hidden inside the neck, it resists the roughly 70 kg combined pull of the six strings and keeps a slight bow in the neck; it should be adjusted by a professional.
80a09cca9e: Extended notes: choosing and caring for a guitar
4db197185f: Never put steel strings on a classical guitar: the pull is too strong and will warp the neck and bridge
cdddf6b7e4: Choose size and body shape to fit your body; a good fit matters more than size
59a41f7663: Sore fingertips for the first two weeks are normal; if the action at string 6, fret 12 is over about 3 mm, have a technician adjust it
debbcb5d4a: Keep it out of sun, heat and humidity; store it in its bag, and watch the humidity in Taiwan's summers
1a442ed6d0: Standard tuning from string 6 to string 1 is E, A, D, G, B, E. Neighbouring strings are a perfect fourth apart, except strings 3 to 2, which are a major third; strings 1 and 6 are two octaves apart. Say it: Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie.
723c3a83bf: How to tune: listen to the reference note → pluck the open string → tightening raises the pitch, loosening lowers it → if it's sharp, loosen below the target first and then tighten slowly back up; it holds its tuning better.
5220481f2e: Extended notes: getting ready to play
93c8359c5b: **Sitting**: sit on the front third of the chair with your back straight; rest the body on your right thigh close to you, with the neck tilted slightly up.
13cf88e3f5: **Holding the pick**: rest it on the side of the first joint of your index finger with the thumb on top, about 2–3 mm of tip showing; let the middle, ring and little fingers relax open, and keep your wrist steady, not twisting, as you strum.
8649be4021: **Finger numbers**: left hand index 1, middle 2, ring 3, little 4; for right-hand fingerpicking, thumb T covers strings 4–6, index 1 string 3, middle 2 string 2, ring 3 string 1.
c3e20f073d: **Left-hand fretting**: press with the area between tip and pad, fingers as upright to the fretboard as possible and close to the fret; keep the thumb on the middle line at the back of the neck, not resting on the fretboard.
